name: Greater Galangal
summary: Greater galangal (Alpinia galanga) is a tropical rhizomatous spice crop distinct from culinary ginger and lesser galangal. UF/IFAS describes warm, Florida-specific production and harvest guidance; it is not a hydroponic or seed-grown profile.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Alpinia galanga in Zingiberaceae. UF/IFAS distinguishes greater galangal from lesser galangal (Alpinia officinarum), fingerroot (Boesenbergia rotunda), and sand ginger (Kaempferia galanga). No cultivar is assigned.

growth.short: Tropical rhizomatous perennial; galangal differs from ginger in seasonal response
growth.guidance: Kew classifies Alpinia galanga as a rhizomatous geophyte of wet tropical biomes. UF/IFAS reports that galangal has not shown photoperiod-induced dormancy; it may flower and produce rhizomes year-round in tropical areas, while flowering is seasonal in subtropics. The source does not establish a portable mature height or spread.

cultivation.short: Warm, moist but aerated growing conditions; UF/IFAS context is Florida production
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS gives 70–85°F as an optimum range for ginger and galangal production and describes 25–40% shade in Florida summers to reduce heat and leaf stress without overshading. Once established in summer, its rhizome crops typically need daily irrigation or rainfall; use a coarse, well-drained substrate that retains moisture. These are Florida crop-production references, not universal household settings, indoor-light targets, or a hydroponic recipe.

propagation.short: Rhizomes or tissue-culture plants are documented planting material
propagation.guidance: UF/IFAS documents starting these crops from rhizomes or tissue-culture plants and identifies galangal as vigorous from tissue culture. The selected source does not document seed propagation, so no seed method is inferred.

harvestUse.short: Harvest fresh rhizomes before they become increasingly fibrous
harvestUse.guidance: UF/IFAS says galangal rhizomes for fresh produce are harvested at about four months after planting in its Florida production context; later harvests become more fibrous. It separately reports about seven months for essential-oil production. The publication discusses fresh sale, preserves, and dried powder, but these dates are not universal home-growing deadlines or cultivar-specific promises.

flowering.short: Flowering season depends on tropical versus subtropical context
flowering.guidance: UF/IFAS reports summer flowering in subtropics and year-round flower and rhizome production in tropical areas, independent of photoperiod. This is regional species-level context, not an indoor bloom calendar.

problems.short: Watch for drought stress and rhizome/root disease risk without overgeneralizing pathogen records
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS describes leaf curling followed by tip or marginal burn and yellowing as drought-stress signs among its rhizome crops, and emphasizes clean planting material, sanitation, and avoiding waterlogging. The listed pathogen detections are specifically reported on Florida-grown ginger and turmeric, not as galangal-specific diagnoses; no resistance claim is made for galangal.

name: Common Sage
variety: Species identity; no named cultivar assigned
summary: A woody perennial culinary herb with aromatic gray-green leaves. Common sage is distinct from pineapple sage and other Salvia species; pruning, harvest and dimensions here remain at species or regional garden-guidance scope.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Salvia officinalis in Lamiaceae. This is common culinary sage, not pineapple sage (S. elegans), clary sage (S. sclarea), or a named leaf-color cultivar.

growth.short: Woody perennial with aromatic, gray-green leaves
growth.guidance: University Extension describes common sage as a woody perennial with oblong, softly textured gray-green leaves and a tendency to become woody with age. The sources describe established garden plants; no indoor-system size is inferred.

cultivation.short: Full sun and very well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: Maryland Extension recommends full sun and very well-drained soil, especially for overwintering. This is outdoor garden guidance and does not define an indoor grow-light tier, hydroponic recipe, or universal watering schedule.

care.short: Prune in spring without cutting into old woody stems
care.guidance: Wisconsin Extension recommends spring and in-season pruning to encourage young shoots and limit leggy, woody growth. It cautions against cutting back into mature woody stems that may not resprout. This is maintenance guidance, not a cultivar-specific pruning formula.

harvest.short: Harvest leaves before flowering; avoid removing more than half at once
harvest.guidance: Wisconsin Extension describes cutting shoots and taking leaves before flowering; it cautions against removing more than half of the plant at once. No first-year harvest schedule is asserted in this profile.

propagation.short: Seed and vegetative routes are documented; named cultivars may not come true from seed
propagation.guidance: Wisconsin Extension lists seed, layering, division and stem cuttings for sage, and notes that many named varieties are vegetatively propagated and may not come true from seed. This species-level profile does not promise a named cultivar from seed; consult the Seed Profile for its establishment evidence.

problems.short: Avoid persistently wet soil and aging woody growth
problems.guidance: Maryland Extension emphasizes very well-drained soil, while Wisconsin Extension describes declining foliage quality as plants become old and woody. These are cultivation concerns; the profile does not assert a disease-resistance trait or diagnose a particular plant.

name: Curry Leaf Tree
variety: Species identity; former scientific synonym Murraya koenigii
summary: A tropical-to-subtropical aromatic shrub or small tree valued for fresh curry leaves in South Asian cooking. Kew accepts Bergera koenigii and lists Murraya koenigii as a synonym; this is not curry powder or a named compact cultivar.

identity.short: Accepted name Bergera koenigii; Murraya koenigii is a synonym
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Bergera koenigii in Rutaceae and lists Murraya koenigii as a synonym, a name still used in horticultural sources. UC Master Gardeners distinguish the plant from curry powder and describe its aromatic leaves as a South Asian culinary staple.

growth.short: Aromatic shrub or small tree; size varies by form and climate
growth.guidance: Kew classifies the species as a shrub, and UC Master Gardeners describe a small tree. The source notes regular, dwarf and compact forms exist but does not identify a cultivar in this profile; no single mature dimension is assigned.

cultivation.short: Protect from frost; allow the soil to dry between waterings
cultivation.guidance: UC Master Gardeners' Santa Clara County guidance describes a perennial that can remain evergreen in Zone 10, may lose leaves in colder microclimates, and should be protected from frost. It recommends well-drained soil and allowing soil to dry between waterings; these are regional recommendations, not a universal container schedule.

light.short: Outdoor exposure ranges from full sun to partial shade
light.guidance: The UC Master Gardener source lists full sun to partial shade and recommends protecting plants from direct summer sun in its local hot-weather context. This is outdoor exposure guidance, not a normalized indoor grow-light requirement.

harvest.short: Pick leaves for fresh use; freezing is preferred to drying in the cited guidance
harvest.guidance: UC Master Gardeners say leaves can be harvested anytime for fresh use and frozen for later; the source cautions that drying reduces flavor. No yield, pruning interval or universal harvest amount is established.

propagation.short: Fresh seed and vegetative methods are documented
propagation.guidance: UC Master Gardeners describe fresh ripe seed, root suckers and cuttings. Seed germination can be erratic and take more than a month in that regional guidance, so the Seed Profile preserves the fresh-seed context and leaves unsupported depth and seedling timing unresolved.

problems.short: Cold and strong summer sun can stress the plant
problems.guidance: The selected regional source warns about frost in colder microclimates and sunburn during hot summer weather. It also notes local Asian citrus psyllid quarantine considerations; those are location-specific regulatory guidance and are not generalized as a universal pest claim here.
